concepts.name: Legal Basis of CBI: DSPE Act vs. Statutory Status
key_dimensions: CBI is NOT created by a statute of its own — it operates under the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946
The name 'CBI' itself has no statutory backing — it was conferred by a Home Ministry Resolution of 1963
Distinction trap: CBI ≠ statutory body in the strict sense, unlike CVC or ED which have explicit statutory mandates
Implications of non-statutory status: no suo motu powers, dependence on consent and notification mechanisms

concepts.name: DSPE Act 1946: Origin, Scope, and Current Relevance
key_dimensions: Originally enacted to investigate cases of bribery/corruption in wartime procurement during British India
Post-independence adoption under Article 372 and its extension to CBI functions
Section 3: Power of Central Government to extend DSPE's jurisdiction to specified offences
Section 5: Extension of powers to Union Territories — basis for CBI's territorial jurisdiction outside Delhi

concepts.name: CBI's Jurisdiction: Three Categories of Cases
key_dimensions: Category 1 — RC (Regular Cases): corruption by central government employees under PC Act
Category 2 — PE (Preliminary Enquiries): cases referred by ministries/courts/own intelligence
Category 3 — Special Crimes: serious crimes like terrorism, bank fraud, organized crime referred by Centre or courts
UPSC trap: CBI cannot take up state-subject crimes suo motu — requires consent or court order

concepts.name: Consent Mechanism: Section 6 of DSPE Act
key_dimensions: Section 6 mandates that CBI must obtain consent of the State Government before investigating in that state
Two types of consent: case-specific (for individual cases) and general consent (blanket for all CBI cases)
Withdrawal of general consent: states like West Bengal, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Kerala have withdrawn — creating a jurisdictional vacuum
Post-withdrawal: CBI needs fresh specific consent each time, weakening federal investigation capacity

concepts.name: Suo Motu Powers of CBI: Scope and Limitations
key_dimensions: CBI has NO suo motu power to register FIR and investigate crimes in states without consent
Contrast with NIA which can suo motu investigate scheduled offences under NIA Act 2008 — a key UPSC distinction
CBI can act suo motu only within Union Territories and in cases involving central government employees on central premises
Supreme Court/High Court can direct CBI to investigate without state consent — judicial override of Section 6

concepts.name: Court-Ordered CBI Investigation: Constitutional and Legal Basis
key_dimensions: Supreme Court power under Article 142 to order CBI investigation — 'complete justice' provision
High Courts under Article 226 can also direct CBI investigation within their territorial jurisdiction
Landmark: Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) — Supreme Court supervised CBI in Hawala scandal, established 'Continuance Mandamus'
Limitation: State consent requirement under Section 6 can be overridden by court order — Kazi Lhendup Dorji case principle

concepts.name: CBI and the Prevention of Corruption Act (PC Act): Jurisdictional Interplay
key_dimensions: CBI is the primary investigating agency for offences under PC Act 1988 involving central government employees
Special Courts under PC Act: designated sessions courts for CBI-investigated corruption cases
Section 17 of PC Act: only a DSP-rank or above CBI officer can investigate — rank requirement trap
Amendment of PC Act 2018: prior sanction now required even for arrest, not just prosecution — impacts CBI operations

concepts.name: Supervision of CBI: Role of CVC
key_dimensions: CVC Act 2003: CVC exercises superintendence over CBI in matters relating to PC Act offences
Distinction: CVC superintendence is limited to anti-corruption cases — NOT all CBI cases
For other cases (special crimes, bank fraud), CBI is supervised by the Ministry of Personnel
Vineet Narain judgment: established that CBI should not be under political executive's thumb — CVC as buffer

concepts.name: Appointment and Removal of CBI Director: Legal Safeguards
key_dimensions: Post-Vineet Narain (1997): CBI Director's tenure fixed at 2 years for insulation from political interference
DSPE Amendment Act 2014 (after Lokpal Act): appointment by committee — PM + Leader of Opposition + CJI
Amendment 2021: tenure extendable up to 5 years total (annual extensions after 2 years) — controversy of extensions
Removal: can only be removed with intimation to appointment committee — not at executive's will

concepts.name: CBI vs. State Police: Federal Tension and Constitutional Position
key_dimensions: 'Police' is a State subject under Schedule VII, List II, Entry 2 — constitutional basis of consent requirement
DSPE Act is valid because it governs a Central force, not state police — Entry 80, List I (extension of powers)
State withdrawal of consent as assertion of federalism vs. Centre's argument of national interest investigations
Landmark: State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010) — SC held High Court can order CBI despite withdrawn consent

concepts.name: CBI Headquarters, Structure, and Divisions
key_dimensions: CBI headquartered in New Delhi; Director is equivalent to DG of Police
Three main divisions: Anti-Corruption Division (AC), Special Crimes Division (SC), Economic Offences Division (EO)
Banking Securities Fraud Cell (BSFC) under Economic Offences — handles large bank frauds
UPSC trap: CBI is under Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions — NOT Ministry of Home Affairs

concepts.name: CBI and Special Courts: Trial Mechanism
key_dimensions: CBI cases tried in Special CBI Courts established under PC Act / Criminal Law Amendment Act 1952
Special Judge appointed by Central Government in consultation with High Court — not regular sessions court
Appeal from Special Court lies directly to High Court — bypassing Sessions Court
Delay in trials: CBI courts overloaded — Supreme Court has repeatedly directed time-bound trials

concepts.name: CBI's Role in Economic Offences: Overlap with ED and SFIO
key_dimensions: CBI investigates under IPC/CrPC; ED investigates under PMLA and FEMA — different legal frameworks for same underlying crime
SFIO (Serious Fraud Investigation Office) under Companies Act 2013 — overlapping jurisdiction in corporate fraud
Twin investigation trap: accused can face simultaneous CBI (criminal) and ED (civil/criminal PMLA) proceedings
Coordination mechanism: MOU between CBI and ED for information sharing — but jurisdictional conflicts remain

concepts.name: Lokpal Act 2013 and CBI: Prosecutorial Independence
key_dimensions: Lokpal Act created a mechanism for Lokpal to refer cases to CBI — CBI to report progress to Lokpal
Amendment ensuring CBI Director's appointment via collegium-type committee inserted via Lokpal Amendment
Debate: should CBI's prosecution wing be separated from investigation? — Law Commission recommendations
Section 26 of Lokpal Act: Lokpal can authorize CBI to conduct preliminary inquiry in cases against public servants

concepts.name: 'Caged Parrot' Controversy: Judicial Observations on CBI Independence
key_dimensions: Supreme Court's observation in Coal Scam case (2013): CBI is a 'caged parrot speaking in its master's voice'
Context: sharing of status reports with Law Ministry/PMO — political interference allegation
Court directions: CBI must not share investigation reports with accused or political executive
Structural reforms suggested: independent prosecution directorate, fixed tenure for all senior officials

concepts.name: CBI Investigation Outside India: Interpol and MLA Treaties
key_dimensions: CBI is India's nodal agency for Interpol — maintains National Central Bureau (NCB) for Interpol coordination
Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs): CBI coordinates requests for evidence/extradition from foreign countries
Distinction: CBI coordinates MLATs but formal extradition requests processed through Ministry of External Affairs
Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018: CBI/ED can attach assets — supplements extradition mechanism

concepts.name: Notification of Offences Under DSPE Act: Section 3 Mechanism
key_dimensions: Section 3: Central Government must notify specific offences that CBI can investigate — not a blanket power
Notification mechanism allows expanding or contracting CBI's subject-matter jurisdiction by executive order
Current notified offences include: corruption under PC Act, economic offences, conventional crimes of national importance
UPSC trap: CBI cannot automatically investigate all central government matters — notification is a prerequisite

concepts.name: High Court Jurisdiction Over CBI: Transfer and Supervisory Powers
key_dimensions: High Court under Article 226 can transfer investigation from state police to CBI within its territorial jurisdiction
Supreme Court under Article 32 + 142 can order CBI investigation anywhere in India irrespective of state consent
Courts cannot direct CBI to investigate crimes that are not notified under Section 3 of DSPE Act — subject-matter limit
Controversy: frequent court-ordered CBI investigations seen as undermining state police — federalism concern

concepts.name: CBI vs. NIA: Comparative Jurisdiction and Powers
key_dimensions: NIA created by NIA Act 2008 — has suo motu power to take up scheduled offences (terrorism, UAPA cases) without state consent
CBI requires state consent (Section 6 DSPE); NIA does NOT — this is a critical UPSC distinction
NIA can investigate across states; set up Special NIA Courts; override state police jurisdiction
Overlap: both can investigate terror-financing, but NIA has primacy under NIA Act for scheduled offences

concepts.name: Proposed Reforms and Pending Legislation for CBI
key_dimensions: Demand for a separate CBI Act to give it statutory independence (similar to FBI in the US context — for comparison)
Second Administrative Reforms Commission: recommended insulating CBI from political control via statutory charter
Law Commission of India reports: suggested separation of investigation and prosecution wings
Parliamentary Standing Committee recommendations: time-bound investigations, independent budget allocation, statutory backing
